title: Tate Brothers Fight UK Extradition as White House Refuses to Intervene
excerpt: Lawyer Joseph McBride calls the extradition bid a 'political witch hunt' and urges Trump to block it, but the White House and Secretary of State Marco Rubio say they have no plans to step in.
body:
• Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 and face 59 total charges in the UK, including rape, sex trafficking, and offences related to indecent images of a child.
  • Their lawyer Joseph McBride has called for President Trump to block the extradition, framing the case as a "political witch hunt" and "political kidnapping."
  • The White House and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have both said they will not intervene, with Rubio stating there is "no role" for the administration to play.
  • A detention hearing is set for August 13, with Britain required to submit its full extradition request to the State Department by September 16.

Andrew and Tristan Tate, the controversial social media influencers arrested in Miami on July 18, are locked in a high-stakes legal battle against extradition to the United Kingdom — and their lawyer's bid to enlist the Trump administration has so far fallen flat.

The brothers, both former kickboxers who hold dual US-British citizenship, were taken into custody by US Marshals following a request from British authorities linked to a sweeping set of criminal charges announced by the UK's Crown Prosecution Service. They appeared before a federal magistrate in Miami wearing tan jail uniforms, handcuffed and shackled at the waist and ankles.

The Charges

The CPS announced 38 new charges against the brothers in addition to 21 existing ones, bringing the total to 59. Andrew Tate, 39, faces seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and 19 additional charges relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography, according to the CPS.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=mWi3VoCEbeE

Tristan Tate, 38, faces one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape, and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The charges relate to alleged offences between July 2010 and August 2017 involving four alleged victims, according to federal filings unsealed on July 20.

The brothers have denied all allegations against them.

Lawyer Invokes Trump, Calls Case 'Political Kidnapping'

Speaking outside the Wilkie D. Ferguson Jr. US Courthouse in Miami, the Tates' attorney Joseph McBride launched a combative defence, calling the charges "salacious and defamatory" and the extradition bid a "political witch hunt."

"You can love them, you can hate them, but nobody should go to jail for free speech, and that is exactly what this is about."

— Joseph McBride, lawyer for the Tate brothers

McBride branded Britain "a fallen state that prosecutes its citizens for free speech" and compared the proceedings to the legal cases once faced by Trump himself. He urged the administration to block the extradition, arguing that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio "are not fans of prosecuting people for free speech" and were "elected to fight against this kind of nonsense."

"I can't see him looking at this with an objective lens and agreeing to a political witch hunt and a political kidnapping," McBride told reporters.

White House and Rubio Push Back

The appeal has gained no traction. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt addressed the question directly at a July 23 press briefing: "No. We've already answered that question," she said when asked if the administration planned to intervene.

Rubio, who would ultimately have to sign off on any extradition if US courts approve it, was equally blunt during a diplomatic trip to the Philippines on July 22. "There's no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever," he told reporters, according to Sky News. "I'm not going to opine on something that's still working through a legal process."

"Ms. Leavitt is great, but she is not the President or the Secretary of State. There is no extradition without the Secretary of State's signature. Until that signature exists, it's all commentary."

— Joseph McBride, in response to the White House, to TMZ

What Happens Next

The brothers' defence team plans to file a motion seeking their release on bail by August 5, according to defence lawyer Jacqueline Perczek. A detention hearing is scheduled for August 13 before US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis, who will decide whether they should remain in federal custody.

Federal prosecutors have argued the Tates should stay jailed, citing flight risk and dangers to the community. McBride rejected the flight-risk claim, noting the brothers had attended all required court hearings in Romania, where they have been under criminal investigation since 2022 on human trafficking allegations. That Romanian case remains active.

Britain has until September 16 to submit its full extradition request to the State Department, according to US court records. A judge would then determine whether the UK has provided sufficient evidence to establish probable cause — a process that could take months. Only after that would Rubio make the final call on extradition.

The Tate brothers have built a large online following promoting views on masculinity and wealth, making them key figures in the so-called "manosphere." Trump courted members of that online ecosystem during the 2024 election, including appearing on podcasts hosted by allies of the Tate brothers. The New York Times reported in December 2025 that the Tates had cultivated connections with Trump allies, including his youngest son Barron Trump, who reportedly communicated with Andrew Tate over Zoom. The Trump administration has denied any connection to the Tates.
nri_angle: The Tate brothers have a significant following among young men across South Asia, making the case closely watched in diaspora communities where debates around masculinity and online influence resonate.
